problem_data.story:
JOURNEY TO THE DEEP PAST
By ADAPTATION


The fossil beds stretched endlessly beneath the red sky of Mars-Prime, humanity's first successful terraformed world. Dr. Eva George stood at the edge of the excavation site, watching the dust devils dance across the ancient lakebed. She had arrived here as a young researcher full of ambition, and now it was all coming to an end.

"I don't see why we have to be here," one of the junior researchers complained. "She's not going to say anything we don't already know."

"She'd better," Dr. Victor Hill said loudly from the row in front. "I've been waiting two years for this announcement."

"Victor, please," his research partner Angela Matthews whispered. "People are staring."

"I don't care if they are," Victor said. "You know that when I commit to something, I follow through. And if I want to speak my mind..."

"The Director is coming. Please be quiet."

Victor looked up. "About time. I haven't got all day to sit here. I have fieldwork to complete."

The researcher to his left whispered, "I bet she's going to tell us it's another delay."

"If she does, I'm going to stand up and say I won't tolerate it anymore."

"Victor," Angela said, "Dr. George can hear you if you're going to talk so loud."

"I hope she does. She's the one keeping us all from completing our research legacy, and I hope she hears me."

"You tell her!" someone called from two rows back.

Dr. Oliver Li, the station administrator, sat in the senior staff section with perfect posture. He was studiously ignoring the junior researchers, limiting his field of vision to the left half of the assembly hall. While Dr. George stood before the podium waiting for silence, Oliver reached back with great dignity and scratched his shoulder blade.

Dr. George was dressed in the full ceremonial robes of the Paleontological Institute. Her boots were polished to a mirror shine. Her silver hair was pulled back in the traditional style of senior field researchers, symbolizing dedication to uncovering Earth's ancient history on new worlds. The baldness of her scalp—a side effect of years of radiation exposure during early terraforming—was worn as a badge of honor. Her crimson cloak, embroidered with the fossils of extinct species, rustled as she moved.

"Colleagues," she said. And then, more loudly, "Colleagues!"

The murmur of conversation died away.

"Colleagues," she repeated. "Last week—Thursday, to be exact—one of the junior researchers came to me with a concern."

"Well, I'll be damned," Victor said loudly.

Dr. George cleared her throat. "It was about the Transition Protocol. That's why I called you all together today." She gazed at a point above and behind the audience.

"It reminds me of the parable of the six Archaeopteryx specimens."

Victor sighed deeply.

"Three, you will recall, were properly preserved. When the Great Curator examined them at the Museum of Natural History, they were brought forth and displayed. 'Curator,' the handlers said, 'we have maintained these specimens perfectly.' The Curator looked at them and saw that it was true. Then she blessed them and had them placed in climate-controlled storage. For which the three specimens remained intact for centuries. But three were improperly stored and exposed to humidity; and these three crumbled to dust within a decade."

Oliver rubbed his nose.

"The moral, my colleagues, is clear: proper procedure ensures longevity. As it says in the Institute Charter, 'Methodology preserves truth.'"

Dr. George adjusted her cloak. "I want you all to remember that principle. I want you to take it with you and reflect on it tonight in your quarters.

"Just as those who came to the Curator with their concerns, one of our researchers came to me. He said: 'Director, I am weary of this project.'

"And I know that. Every one of you—every single one—is weary of this project. I know that as well as I know my own name.

"But because he came to me and said, 'Director, I am weary of this project,' I went to the administrator, and I said, 'Administrator, the team is weary.'

"And then Oliver said: 'Very well, Director. I will set the date for the Transition Ceremony!'"

The small woman was pleased by the rustle of approval from the audience. "About damn time!" Victor said.

Dr. George cleared her throat again. "And the date is not far off," she said.

"I knew there was a catch," Victor muttered.

"I know you will have many questions. You are thinking: 'What kind of ceremony can we have here on this station?' You are thinking: 'How wonderful it would be to have the Transition at home, among colleagues from other institutions.'

"Well, I want to tell you: I come from the Meadowbrook Region research facilities. And you know that Meadowbrook never let any other region outdo them in a Transition Ceremony.

"The amphitheater in Meadowbrook is the greatest in the whole system. We have had as many as sixty thousand participants in our institutional reforms. All of them together—it's quite a sight. People come from everywhere to witness it. I'll never forget the ceremony when my mentor transitioned. She...

"Well, my point is this: I know what a proper Transition should be, and Oliver and I will do everything in our power to make ours as meaningful as any anywhere.

"And I want you to know that if you come to me with your suggestions, I'll do all I can to see that we honor our professional ethics properly. I want you to be proud of this Transition Ceremony, so you can look back on it and say—this was the real culmination of your research career!"

Everyone but Victor cheered. He sat glumly muttering to himself.

Dr. George nodded at them and beamed. She noticed that there was a young woman, one of the junior researchers, in the front row who had very promising field notes.

While they were still cheering, Dr. George walked off the platform and into the senior staff corridor. She wiped her forehead on her sleeve and felt relieved that the announcement was over.

---

Dinner that evening was a celebration in the station. The kitchen staff prepared a feast in honor of Dr. George's announcement. For the senior staff, Oliver broke out the last case of vintage Thornhill wine from Havencia ('94). He ordered it placed at each setting.

Oliver came down from his office after the meal had begun. He nodded curtly to the staff when he entered the dining hall, walked directly to his place at the head of the table, and began working the cork out of his wine bottle.

"You'll spoil the flavor, shaking it that way," Dr. Nicole Leonard cautioned. She was particularly fond of that vintage.

Oliver twisted the bottle, and the cork came free with a pop. He placed it carefully beside his fork and poured himself a full glass.

"Very probably," he said sadly.

"I don't think it'll matter," Dr. Elizabeth Holt said. "He hasn't shaken it hard enough."

Oliver picked up the glass, brought it toward his lips—then suddenly put it back down and turned to Dr. George.

"Director. Have you decided on the Hill matter yet?"

The small paleontologist looked up. She laid her knife across her plate. "It has complications," she said.

When Nicole saw that her opinion on the wine was not to be immediately validated, she settled back with a small sigh.

"What do you think your decision will be, Director?" the kitchen supervisor asked.

Dr. George cut a piece of meat. "It's difficult to say. The whole issue involves, as a core point, the principle of personal growth versus institutional loyalty."

Elizabeth nodded knowingly.

"The intent, of course, could be interpreted as prioritizing individual achievement over collaborative research; and in that case, naturally, the decision would be even more complex. I wish I could consult with the Institute Council, but there isn't time. I'll have to decide something."

"He had very impressive field notes," Nicole said.

"Yes, very," Dr. George agreed. "But as I was saying, if it could be proven that his departure from protocol was due to no negligence on his part, either conscious or unconscious, then obviously no professional sanctions would apply." She chewed thoughtfully.

"But the data wasn't compromised at all," Angela Matthews said. "I don't think the specimens suffered. It happened too quickly."

Dr. George swallowed and washed it down with wine. "The problem, Angela, is one of intent. To focus on the outcome is to miss the point. Take the Wilson case, back in Meadowbrook. Certainly his research was valuable."

"Yes," Angela said. "I read about it in the journals."

"But it was a case of obvious intent to circumvent peer review," continued Dr. George, "and therefore constituted a clear attempt to avoid proper scientific collaboration."

Upon hearing the phrase "proper procedure," Oliver brightened.

"That," he said to Dr. George, "is the cardinal point of the whole matter. Procedure. And I must say, I think you're being quite shortsighted about the Transition date. After all, it's not only a question of how we transition, but also a question of completing our duties first. That's equally important."

"The Institute Charter—" Dr. George began.

"Director! Really. The Institute Charter! Surely you've misinterpreted that. Anticipation can be motivating, you know—almost equal to the achievement itself. Anticipation should drive us in our work. It's noble and purposeful." He scratched his hand.

Elizabeth had been trying to interject for several minutes. "You don't need to worry about your transition, Oliver. I have in mind a most elegant protocol."

Oliver was not visibly cheered; he was still brooding about the lack of urgency regarding proper procedure. "I will welcome it," he said, "at the appropriate time. And I certainly hope—" His eyes swept the table. "I certainly hope to be transitioned by a senior researcher. It would be quite improper to have a junior staff member do it."

"Oh, very," said the supervisor.

"I don't know," Angela said, "whether you can count on my participation. I have my own research to complete."

"This question of Victor Hill interests me," Nicole said. "I was telling my husband just yesterday—it's been a long time since I saw such flagrant disregard for protocol."

"He was very ambitious," her husband said.

"He probably wouldn't have succeeded anyway," Nicole said. "Flawed methodology."

"That," said Dr. George, "is not at all like the Hill case. Not at all. Yours is a question of labor relations and attribution."

Elizabeth nodded.

"It seems to me the whole thing depends on his intent."

"Oliver," the supervisor said, "you really must try some of this bread."

"That's very kind, but I..."

"No trouble at all," the supervisor said.

"As I see it," Dr. George said, "if the intent was natural competitive drive to advance his career, then..."

"Oh, not at all," Nicole said. "He did it because he wanted the recognition."

"Well, in that case, I see no reason why he shouldn't receive credit."

"I certainly hope so," Nicole's husband said. "She worries about it constantly."

"I do not," Nicole contradicted.

"Now, dear, you know you do."

At that moment, Nicole lost interest and leaned toward Oliver. "Well?" she asked.

Oliver rolled the wine over his tongue. "You were right, of course."

Nicole turned triumphantly to Elizabeth. "There, I told you."

Elizabeth shrugged. "I never get anything right. I've been here nearly fifteen years myself, building a research portfolio that's better than even Oliver's. And Angela and I have to stay and help orient the next team. Lord knows how long before we get our own Transition."

"Really, now. Duty, duty," Oliver reprimanded mildly.

"Duty! Duty! Duty! You're all conspiring against me. You want me to die of old age before I can complete my life's work."

"Nonsense," said the supervisor. "We don't want that. After all, someone has to train the newcomers."

"Quite right," said Oliver. "You should be honored."

Elizabeth threw her napkin on her plate and left the dining hall.

"Quite sensitive today," Dr. George observed. "Though I understand her frustration. When I first proposed this program, I never imagined the bureaucratic delays we'd face."

"By the way," Nicole said, "Lucy Hicks gave me a petition for you, Director."

"Lucy?"

"Yes. She's twenty-four now."

"Lucy who?" the supervisor asked.

"Lucy Hicks, from the geology team."

"I know her," Angela said.

"She's the youngest researcher on the station, and she wants you to approve her participation in the Transition, Director."

"She's so young..."

"Twenty-four, Director."

"After all, one must have completed significant research," Oliver said.

"She wants to participate in the Knowledge Transfer," Nicole said.

Dr. George fidgeted uncomfortably. "Well, I'll review her publication record," she said.

"It's necessary," Elizabeth's husband said. "Otherwise, we'll be short one researcher for the pairing."

"There wouldn't be a shortage if he had brought a research partner," Elizabeth said, glaring at Oliver.

"Now, Elizabeth. I prioritize institutional duty over personal convenience. You're just frustrated because you have to continue with your current assignment."

"All right, I am. But it's true. And if that accident in Sector Seven hadn't happened, we'd be short two." She shot a look at Dr. George. "Why don't you two share a research line—"

"Elizabeth!"

"Although heaven knows what researcher in their right mind would consent to..."

"Well," said Dr. George hesitantly.

"Listen," Nicole said, "Elizabeth's right. If you don't approve it, someone will have to work without a partner."

Dr. George blushed. "I'll review it carefully, but you must understand that senior researchers..."

"Actually, in a way, it would be her duty, you see. Think of it as her contribution to the project."

"She's too young for you, dear," Nicole said to her husband.

"Oh, I don't know," the supervisor said. "Sometimes the young ones are the most innovative."

---

Nicole's husband, whose name was Dr. Fatima Parker, stood before the mirror adjusting his collar. He had been fussing with his appearance for fifteen minutes.

"I suppose the junior staff is celebrating?" Nicole said.

"I suppose."

She stood and walked to the desk, absently fingering the research notes there.

"You really shouldn't have mentioned that student tonight."

"Nonsense."

"No, Fatima. I mean it. Angela looked at me strangely all through dinner. She has three major publications, you know."

"You're imagining things."

"But she does have three publications."

"I mean about her looking at you."

"Oh."

Fatima adjusted his tie without speaking.

"I mean, as much as to say: 'Well, I properly credited all my collaborators.'"

"But honey, about the student. That was nearly an accident. You didn't really mean to exclude him from authorship."

"But still... Angela looked at me like I wasn't following proper professional ethics."

"No," he said. "That's nonsense, Nicole. You know what the Director said."

He polished one of his Institute pins with his sleeve.

"Fatima?"

"Yes?"

"I don't think all that preparation is necessary just for field research."

"Probably not."

She sat on the bed. "Fatima?"

"Yes, dear?"

"Don't you really think she's too young?"

"Not really."

"I mean, why don't you choose someone else? Like Mary from the chemistry lab? She's accomplished. I bet she'd be better."

"Probably."

"She's very collaborative."

He brushed at his hair again. "Who do you want as your partner, Nicole?"

"Oh, I don't know." She looked at her hands. "I think I'd like to work with Dr. George. With her impressive publication record—all those years establishing this program. I hope she asks me."

"I'll mention it to her."

"Would you really, Fatima? That would be wonderful."

"Sure, honey." He looked at his watch.

"Fatima? Are you going to meet Lucy in the laboratory?"

"Yes."

"I thought so. Well, remember: It isn't the day of the Knowledge Transfer yet. Don't forget."

"Honey! You don't think for a minute that..."

"No, dear. I know you wouldn't. But just don't."

He kissed her forehead and patted her cheek. "Of course not," he said comfortingly.

He left her sitting on the bed and walked down the senior corridor, whistling.

He made a mental note to have maintenance clean these walls tomorrow. They needed it. In one corner a spider had spun its web.

He climbed the stairs, turned left, and felt the fresh air from the ventilation system.

Beneath it lay one of the junior researchers, asleep.

He nudged the person several times until consciousness returned.

"Can't sleep here," Fatima explained.

"Go away and leave me alone."

"Here, now." He helped the fellow up and steadied him. "This is the senior corridor."

"Oh? Sorry. So sorry, sir."

Fatima assisted him to the junior corridor where he sank down and fell asleep again.

Fatima continued to the laboratory.

When he entered, Nicole's colleague was yawning.

"Hi, John. Tired?"

"Yes. You're early."

"Don't mind, do you?"

"No... Quiet tonight. Had to shut down the carbon dating equipment an hour ago. The technician was incapacitated."

"Oh?"

John lit a cigarette. "Can't risk contaminating the samples. Would look terrible in the research record. Hope Oliver doesn't find out. He'll think the technician was neglecting duty."

He blew a smoke ring.

"Might even bar him from the Transition."

"Yeah," said Fatima, "Oliver's particular that way."

John blew another smoke ring.

"Well," Fatima said.

"Uh. Fatima? Are you really going to partner with that Lucy Hicks?"

"If Dr. George approves."

"Say, Fatima. Do you suppose Nicole would...?"

Fatima put a hand on John's shoulder. "Sorry, old friend. She's set on working with Dr. George." He shrugged. "I don't entirely approve, but... I'm sure if the Director declines, she'd be glad to consider your proposal."

"That's all right," John said. "Doesn't really matter. Say, have I told you what I'm planning for Oliver's transition protocol? I've thought it all through. You know that ceremonial fossil I acquired on the expedition to Pinehurst in Wendria? Well..."

"How about telling me another time?"

"Oh. Sure. If you prefer."

"I'm expecting Lucy."

"Oh. Right. I should have known you weren't here early for nothing. In that case, I'll be going. Good luck."

"Thanks. See you at breakfast."

"Right."

After John left, Fatima walked to the control panel. The dating equipment was dark. He picked up the intercom and called the technical staff. "Hello, this is Dr. Parker... Oh, hi, Barney. Do you have a sober technician available yet...? Good. We'll restart the equipment. If Oliver comes by now—well, you know how he is.... Okay, thanks. Good night."

He replaced the receiver and threw the power switch. The equipment hummed to life.

Having done that, he activated the holographic display system. The steady hum of the equipment warming filled the room. Lucy would certainly want to examine the fossil reconstructions. She was enthusiastic about such things.

"Hello."

He turned. "Oh, hello, Lucy."

"Hello, Dr. Parker. Are you glad I could come?"

"Very much."

"Me too. Can I look at the—oh, it's already on."

"Yes. Look, Lucy."

"Hmm?"

"I spoke to Dr. George today."

"Wonderful. What did she say? Can I participate in the Transition as an adult researcher?"

"I don't know yet. She's reviewing your record. That's why I wanted to see you. She's going to check your publications. And Lucy?"

"Those reconstructions are beautiful."

"Lucy, listen to me."

"I'm listening, Dr. Parker."

"You're simply going to stop carrying around that stuffed toy if you want to be taken seriously as an adult researcher."

---

In Dr. George's office the next morning, Oliver and the Director held a conference. The walls displayed various certificates and photographs chronicling the program's history—Dr. George as a young woman standing beside the first excavation site, group photos from subsequent expeditions marking the passing years.

"No, Oliver. I'm afraid I can't agree to that," Dr. George said.

Oliver said, "Oh, don't be unreasonable, Director. After all, this is a research station. And I am, after all, the administrator."

Dr. George shook her head. "The junior and senior staff will participate together in the Transition. I will not segregate the corridors, and—Oh! Yes? Come in!"

The door opened. "Director?"

"Yes? Come in."

"Thank you, Director. Good morning, Administrator."

"Sit down. Now, Oliver, as I was saying: no segregation. It's contrary to the spirit, if not the letter, of the Institute Charter."

"But Director! A junior researcher! In the senior corridor! Consider the implications!"

"Before the Institute, we are all equal. I'm sorry, Oliver. Now in Meadowbrook, we practiced it with excellent results, and..."

"I say, really—"

"Director?" said the junior researcher who had entered.

"Yes? One moment. Now, Oliver. As I've been explaining: The traditional amphitheater method has advantages. In Meadowbrook we always used it. But here—due to the constraints of the station—I feel convinced that a modification of normal procedure is warranted. It's not without precedent. Such adaptations were fairly common during the early colonial period, up until the Institute standardization three hundred years ago. Indeed, in Meadowbrook, during the outbreak of Martian fever, a most unusual protocol was adopted. It seems..."

"You're perfectly correct, of course," Oliver said.

"That's what I wanted to discuss, Director," the junior researcher said. "Now, in Bayview, Veldoria, for the Transitions, we..."

"Please be quiet," said Oliver softly.

"Yes, sir."

"Now, as I was saying, Oliver, when the methods used in..."

"If you'll excuse me, Director, I really should return to my research," the junior researcher said.

"Quite all right. Close the door after you."

"I must say, your dedication is commendable."

"Well, thank you, sir. And thank you, Director, for your time."

"Not at all. That's what I'm here for. Come by anytime."

The researcher closed the door.

He had barely left when Fatima Parker knocked and was admitted.

"Oh? Good morning, Oliver. I didn't know you were here." Then, to the Director: "I'll return later."

"Nonsense," said Oliver. "Come in."

"Well, I hoped to see the Director privately."

"I should be going," said Oliver.

"But Oliver! I haven't finished explaining about..."

"I'll just get some coffee," Oliver said.

"I'll call you when I'm finished," said Fatima.

Oliver left the room.

"It's about Lucy, Director," Fatima said.

The Director studied her desk, glancing at the old mission logs stacked beside her. She rearranged some papers. "Ah, yes. The young researcher."

"Well, it's not only about Lucy," said Fatima. "You see, my wife, Nicole..."

"Yes?" The Director picked up her pen.

"I think, with the proper encouragement, she might be interested in collaborating with you in the Knowledge Transfer, if I put in a good word."

"That is very flattering." She returned the pen to its holder. "Such generosity, as it says in the Charter, promotes cultural exchange."

"And with your permission, Director..."

"Ah..."

"She's a very accomplished researcher."

"Ah... Quite so."

"Well, about Lucy. I really shouldn't mention this. But Director, if we are short one researcher for the pairing..."

"Hmm."

"I mean, it wouldn't be fair to the others."

"I see your point." Dr. George blinked. "It wouldn't be equitable, all things considered."

She stood up.

"I may tell you that, in reviewing this matter last night, I decided that Lucy Hicks has completed sufficient research to merit participation in the Transition."

"Professional ethics are a virtue of good directors," Fatima said.

"And you really think Nicole would...?"

"Oh, yes, Director."

"Well, ahem. But..."

"Yes, Director?"

"There is one small complication."

"Oh?"

"That is to say, in order for a researcher to participate in the Knowledge Transfer ritual, she must be formally paired with a senior colleague."

"I hadn't thought of that," Fatima said disappointedly.

"I think that can be arranged, however," said Dr. George. "If you pass the dining hall on your way out, please tell Oliver we can continue our discussion at his convenience."

---

"Sit down, Oliver," said Dr. George when he returned. "No, over there, in the comfortable chair. Are you comfortable?"

"Of course."

"Good. I have a question for you, Oliver."

"Oh?"

Dr. George rubbed her silver hair. "Sir, I know you have the greatest sensitivity regarding matters of institutional duty."

"That's quite true. I take pride in it, if I may say so."

"Exactly. No sacrifice is too great for the advancement of knowledge."

"True, true."

"Well then, say the first of next month, that would be a Monday—I may depend upon you to formally pair with Lucy Hicks, the junior researcher, yes?"

"No," said Oliver.

"Come now, sir. I realize she is quite junior, but—"

"Director," said Oliver, "did I ever tell you about the time I led the expedition to the fossil beds of Thornhill?"

"I don't believe you have."

"Then I will. It came about this way. I was given command of fifty-three researchers. Brilliant minds. Unconventional, but excellent scientists. I was to lead them ninety-seven kilometers across terrain that..."

"Oliver! I fear I must be very direct with you. I will be forced to announce in the dining hall this evening that you have refused to fulfill your institutional duty when it was plainly and properly presented to you."

"Very well, Director," Oliver said after several minutes. "I will do it."

He was trembling slightly.

---

That morning was to be the time of Oliver's formal pairing. He had insisted it be done privately. For the ceremony, he refused to make any change in his everyday attire; nor would he consent to Dr. George's suggestion that he wear the ceremonial Institute medallion. He had intended, after the ceremony, to return to his duties as if nothing unusual had happened; but afterward, the vast indignity of it struck him more poignantly than he had imagined.

Without a word, he left Dr. George's office and walked slowly, deliberately, with great dignity, to his own quarters.

They were fine quarters. The finest, except for Dr. George's, in the whole station. The curtains were scented with subtle fragrance. The carpet was plush.

He walked through his office without breaking stride.

The bed was large and inviting, an unbroken expanse of white coverlet extending from the far wall. It looked supremely comfortable.

Without even a sigh, he threw himself upon it and lay very, very still. His left leg remained suspended in the air at a forty-five-degree angle to the bed; the angle remained rigidly, unrelaxingly forty-five degrees.

Only after a long time did he roll onto his back, and then merely to stare fixedly at the ceiling.

He might have lain there indefinitely had his introspection not been interrupted, around noon, by an apologetic knock on the door.

"Come in," he whispered, hoping she wouldn't hear and would leave.

But she heard him.

"Partner," Lucy said simply. She closed the door and stood staring at him.

"Miss Hicks," he said, "I hope you will have the courtesy not to use that term again."

"Gosh. You say the funniest things. I'm so glad you had to pair with me."

Oliver stood up, adjusted his jacket and shoulders, and walked to his desk. He opened a drawer, removed a bottle, poured himself half a glass and drank it.

"Ah," he said.

He returned to the bed and sat down.

"Can't you even say hello to me?" she asked.

"Hello," he said. "Miss Hicks, sit down. I intend to give you an instructive lecture on the natural order of institutional hierarchy and..."

"Huh?"

"Ah," he said. "Quite right, of course."

She walked to the chair and sat. "I don't like those," she said, pointing at the curtains.

"Those, Miss Hicks," he said, "are priceless drapes imported from Thornhill, Havencia. They have a fascinating history.

"About three thousand years ago, a family of weavers was forced to flee their city because the eldest son had become involved in a conspiracy against the local governor. As the family was traveling..."

"I don't like them anyway," said Lucy.

"Miss Hicks," said Oliver, "kindly bring me that."

"This?"

"Yes. Thank you."

He took the stuffed toy from her. He stood up again, walked to his desk, searched for scissors. Finally he located them under a stack of research papers.

He looked at the toy, then at Lucy, then back at the toy. With deliberate precision, he began to cut.

---

Later that evening, Dr. George sat alone in her office, reviewing the personnel files one final time before the Transition. The station felt quieter now, expectant.

She pulled out a worn leather journal—her personal log from the early days. The binding was cracked and weathered, the pages yellowed with age. She had started it when she'd been barely older than Lucy was now. A faded label on the cover read "Field Notes: Year One."

She flipped through, watching the entries accumulate. The first pages were filled with youthful enthusiasm—sketches of the crater she'd selected for the initial excavation, notes on soil composition, plans for the station that existed then only in her imagination.

A knock interrupted her reverie.

"Come in."

It was Nicole. "Director, I wanted to ask you about the Knowledge Transfer pairing. Fatima mentioned..."

"Yes, of course." Dr. George set the journal aside. "I've been thinking about my time here, Nicole. All these years building something from nothing."

"You've accomplished so much, Director. The program wouldn't exist without you."

Dr. George smiled faintly. "Do you remember when Elizabeth arrived? She mentioned at dinner she's been here nearly fifteen years now."

"Has it really been that long? I remember meeting her when I first transferred in. She seemed so established already."

"Oliver came five years before Elizabeth did. He likes to remind people of his seniority." Dr. George chuckled softly. "Though he was practically a child when he arrived—younger than Lucy is now, if you can believe it."

Nicole nodded. "I've heard him mention it. He seems to take great pride in his tenure here."

"As well he should. He's been a capable administrator." Dr. George paused, her fingers tracing the edge of her old journal. "When Oliver first stepped off the transport, the excavation protocols were barely established. I'd spent a decade building the foundation of this program before he even arrived—just me and a handful of graduate students, working out of prefab shelters."

"The early years must have been difficult."

"They were. But rewarding." Dr. George turned back to Nicole. "About the pairing—yes, I would be honored to work with you for the Knowledge Transfer. Your research on Martian sediment layers has been exemplary."

Nicole's face lit up. "Thank you, Director. I won't disappoint you."

After Nicole left, Dr. George returned to her journal. She turned to a later section—expedition logs from when the program had finally gained Institute recognition. The entries here were more confident, more assured. She had been in her prime then.

She flipped forward again, past Oliver's arrival, past the construction of the new laboratory wing, past Elizabeth's first field season. The handwriting grew slightly less steady in recent years, the entries more sparse.

---

The next morning, Dr. George found Oliver waiting outside her office, holding a stack of administrative documents.

"Director, I need your signature on these supply requisitions."

"Of course, Oliver. Come in."

As she reviewed the papers, Oliver stood stiffly by the window, gazing out at the excavation site. "You know," he said, "I was thinking about what you said yesterday. About the traditional amphitheater method."

"Oh?"

"It reminded me of the ceremony I attended as a young man, just before I came here. The pageantry was remarkable." He paused. "That was twenty years ago now. Hard to believe."

Dr. George signed the last document and set down her pen. "Time passes strangely when you're devoted to your work."

"Indeed." Oliver gathered his papers. "I suppose I've spent my entire adult life on this station. Sometimes I forget there was anything before it."

After he left, Dr. George turned to the window herself. The red dust swirled in familiar patterns across the lakebed. She remembered watching it from this same window when the glass was newly installed, when the station was still being built around her.

She picked up her journal again, turning to a page near the middle. An entry from the year Oliver arrived—she'd written about her new administrator, her hopes that he would help bring order to the growing program. She'd been running things alone for so long by then.
